title: do you log the trades your bot skips, or are you flying blind like i was?
author: CryptographerBig7624
selftext:
for months i only logged the trades my system actually took. and i kept staring at a break-even curve wondering where the edge was hiding. then it hit me that every setup my bot rejected, i had zero record of. i had no idea if my filter had edge or was just reducing how often i traded. completely different things and i couldn't tell them apart.

so i started logging the skips. every setup that almost qualified but got filtered out, i tracked what it would have done, same exit rules and same time horizon as my real trades. that horizon part matters, a skip that "would have won" three days later means nothing if your real trades close in an hour.

the uncomfortable part: some of my filters were saving me from losers, but a couple were killing trades that would have printed. i was proud of those filters. they were costing me money.

so here's my actual question, do you track your skips at all? and if you do, have you ever found a filter you were proud of that turned out to be costing you? because that one stung and i want to know if it's common

comments.author: Cryshus
comments.body:
I log everything. Mine polls the market every 20 seconds to make a decision. Even after making the decision it will continue to poll the market and say what it would have done that time.

Everything gets logged and this way I can run backtests extremely easily. Anytime I want to add a new feature or see if something would have helped I already have the needed data.

This is specifically for the 15 min btc price prediction.

replies.author: CryptographerBig7624
replies.body: nice, the "keep polling after the decision" bit is clean, most people log the fill and nothing else. one thing worth checking on that setup though, continuous polling tells you what the price did but not what your exit rules would've done to a skipped trade. logging "it went up 0.4% after i passed" is different from "if i'd entered, my stop or tp would've closed it here for +X". the second one is the real counterfactual. are you replaying your actual exit logic on the skips or just tracking raw price after?

replies.author: Cryshus
replies.body:
If by exit logic you mean closing the trade then no. My model either skips a prediction or buys yes/no. I did quite a bit of testing for early exit and for stop loss and it resulted in worse overall performance.

And logs after a decision is made are treated as if no decision was made. Fresh look every 20 seconds. Once the first assessment passes my gates then it's sent off to the market.

So now my model is just buy and hold until that prediction marketing settles.

I've been working on it for the last month or two and have had it live for the past few weeks. It's now consistently having green days. That all circles back to having a logs on everything every 20 sec. Being able to have AI backrest on my logs instead of having to wait for enough samples has helped tremendously.

I am also very new to Ai trading and have no coding background, so apologies if im misunderstanding your question.

replies.author: CryptographerBig7624
replies.body:
ah that makes sense, if it settles at a fixed point there's no exit to replay, the outcome is just the outcome. my question was aimed at systems with discretionary exits, doesn't apply to yours. binary prediction that settles on its own is actually a cleaner measurement problem, you don't have exit noise muddying the signal.

the one thing i'd still watch on the skips: when your model passes on a prediction, do you check whether the ones it skipped would've settled green or red? that's the same question just without the exit part. tells you if your gate is filtering out real losers or also killing winners you'd have wanted. sounds like you've got the data for it already.

green days consistently after a couple months is a good sign btw, most people don't get there

replies.author: Cryshus
replies.body:
Ah ok. I'd have to look into that to be honest. In order for my model to make a trade it has to be at 95% certainty. So there surely are times it gets to 94% then makes no trade. I haven't specifically checked if those cases exist and how much im leaving on the table by excluding them.

What made my model profitable was setting confidence to 95%, originally I had it set to 70%. At 70% it would trade just about every single market. It was only paper trading at this time, but it would have some very good days where it would be up over 100%. But then it would also have days where it would drain a $1000 wallet to 0 in no time.

But this is very insightful and I will have to dig into it! Thank you for sharing your knowledge!

replies.author: CryptographerBig7624
replies.body:
that 70 to 95 jump is a great example of exactly this btw. you already proved the filter works by tightening it, the skip-tracking is just the next layer, it tells you if 95 is actually the sweet spot or if you're leaving good trades on the table at like 93. might turn out 95 is perfect, might turn out 92 captures more without adding the blowup risk. only your logs know.

anyway good talk, you clearly know what you're doing for someone who calls himself new. good luck with it
